items.summary: Radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) is a promising device authentication technique for the Internet of Things (IoT) that leverages hardware impairments to uniquely identify devices. However, most existing RFFI systems operate under a closed-set assumption and lack the ability to detect rogue devices, which poses significant security risks. In this paper, we propose an open-set RFFI approach that jointly performs rogue device detection and legitimate device classification. Specifically, we designed a multi-task RFFI system that integrates an autoencoder (AE) for rogue device detection and a fully connected (FC) layer for classification. To enrich the feature representation, we generated two channel-independent spectrograms (CISs) with distinct window lengths from the I/Q signals, capturing complementary time-frequency characteristics. These CISs were processed in parallel by two Vision Transformer (ViT) networks, and their outputs were fused via feature concatenation to construct a device fingerprint for both tasks. We built a testbed involving ten legitimate LoRa devices and five rogue devices. We conducted a comprehensive experimental evaluation and compared our approach with several benchmark algorithms. Experimental results show that our fused feature multi-task RFFI consistently outperformed the baselines in both legitimate device classification and rogue device detection. Our proposed approach achieved an accuracy of 91.1% and an area under the curve (AUC) of over 0.72 in a realistic wireless scenario where the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) was 20 to 30 dB.
items.title: Open-Set Radio Frequency Fingerprint Identification with Feature Fusion and Vision Transformer

items.summary: This article presents a technical and theoretical assessment of the Quantum-Entangled Neuro-Symbolic Swarm Federation (QENSSF), a framework intended for privacy-preserving, quantum-secure, AI-powered, multimodal healthcare data analysis, introduced by Ben Othman and Ali (2025). Our examination of quantitative support for these claims identified various concerns. Most importantly, the security criterion of a central guarantee (Theorem 1) cannot be satisfied given the risk formulation and relevant constraints, which, along with calculation errors in the proof, directly undermines the claim of provable security. Furthermore, insufficient reporting of biomedical datasets and unresolved discrepancies in the hardware evaluation limit verification of the experimental claims and overall reproducibility. QENSSF identifies a real need: ensuring privacy and security of healthcare data while patients benefit from AI-powered analysis. This need is particularly pressing for sensitive neural data, including the neuroimaging data available through sources such as ADNI. Privacy concerns also extend to wearable EEG data, for which reidentification risks can persist despite deidentification. However, QENSSF's foundational inconsistencies need resolution before it could be considered in the neurosecurity domain.

items.summary: Most resource estimates for breaking secp256k1 with Shor's algorithm describe one long run per attempt, and the spacetime volume of that run, its peak number of logical qubits times its Toffoli count, sets its logical-error budget. Ekerå's tradeoff shrinks each run by using more runs, but how far it can shrink the largest run, and at what circuit cost, has not been determined. We minimize the volume of the largest run while every key is recovered with probability at least 0.99, within ten times the total volume of three runs of Häner et al.\ and $2^{40}$ classical operations. We prove that a linear run fixed in advance, which starts its group register at a point and discards its label, reveals at most $\log_2(1+(|S|-1)/r)$ bits about a uniform key, where $|S|$ counts its exponent values and $r$ is the group order. With generic post-processing and the baseline's window costs, splitting alone then shrinks the largest run at most 1.86 times within the budget. To gain more, we make each exponent bit cheaper with windows that share one table point among exponent values related by six symmetries of the curve, on a point-addition core borrowed from the ECDSA.Fail leaderboard. One random scalar and one random start per run give every approximate addition uniform operands, and a bound on each run's outcomes certifies, for every key, a decoder that discards flagged runs. We count every Toffoli gate and every qubit of every run, and each configuration solved all 563 of its pre-registered simulated trials on secp256k1. The best one shrinks the largest run 3.87 times at 8.79 times the baseline's total volume, against 2.81 times for Ekerå's tradeoff on the same core, and its run is at least 2.6 times smaller than every design of Initio Intelligence.

items.summary: Recent research has investigated fair transaction ordering in blockchain consensus. An orthogonal line of work has demonstrated that equipping replicas with trusted execution environments (TEEs) enables more efficient consensus protocols with only $2f{+}1$ replicas. In this work, we bridge these two areas and demonstrate that two key fair-ordering properties, ordering linearizability and $γ$-batch-order fairness with minimal batching, cannot be implemented in partially synchronous networks with $2f{+}1$ replicas, even when the replicas are equipped with TEEs. We show that Byzantine replicas can circumvent TEE protections by manipulating the timing of transaction submissions to the enclave, thereby biasing the resulting ordering indicators. However, we prove that assuming a synchronous network allows both properties to be implemented with a reduced replica count. We propose two mechanisms: one uses absolute TEE-attested timestamps to guarantee ordering linearizability in a system of $n \ge 2f{+}1$ replicas, and the other uses TEE-maintained relative sequence numbers to guarantee $γ$-batch-order fairness when $n > \frac{2γf}{2γ-1}$. Ultimately, we integrate these mechanisms into a synchronous lane-based consensus algorithm, achieving strong fair-ordering properties and superior performance while requiring fewer replicas than representative state-of-the-art baselines.
items.title: Pearl: TEE-Enabled Fair Ordering with Minimal Replication

items.summary: We study message authentication over a public channel against a computationally unbounded adversary. Motivated by low-complexity applications, we consider schemes that leverage off-the-shelf binary linear codes already used for error correction in communication systems. Existing code-based constructions derive an authentication tag primarily from a single symbol in a $q$-ary code, which limits the tag length. However, selecting several binary coordinates allows a fixed binary linear code to support different tag lengths. We characterize how coordinate selection and ordering affect the statistical guarantees against impersonation and substitution attacks. In particular, we explore three methods: the subset selector, the ordered selector, and the independent selector. They read uniformly chosen coordinates in a fixed public or a secret random order, or with replacement, and add a uniform mask. With a fresh key per message, all three achieve the optimal impersonation probability $2^{-l_t}$ for $l_t$-bit tags. We bound the subset selector's substitution probability using only nonzero weights. Those of the other two depend only on the code length $n$, $l_t$, and the nonzero weight farthest from $n/2$. The independent selector achieves $2^{-l_t}$ for substitution when all nonzero weights equal $n/2$. Finally, we evaluate first-order Reed-Muller and Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem dual subcodes.
items.title: Code-Based Message Authentication with Statistical Guarantees via Coordinate Selection and Masking

items.summary: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.
items.title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment

items.summary: Runtime controls for tool-using agents depend on manifests that state what each tool may read and where its output may go. Evaluations of these controls, including ChainCaps, report per-attack blocking: the share of attacks a set of manifests stops. We show that this is the wrong unit. A catalog is only as safe as its weakest source policy: if $M$ independently authored policies are each wrong with probability $p$, the chance that the catalog contains an accepted exfiltration path is $1-(1-p)^M$, while per-attack blocking stays at $1-p$. Three lines of evidence agree. In synthetic catalogs run through two enforcement engines, ChainCaps and OpenAPPA, per-attack blocking holds at 92% while catalog vulnerability rises from 22% at 10 tools to 99% at 200, and composition provides no protective effect. A fifteen-model authoring pilot shows that real errors cluster by author, so a 200-tool catalog behaves like about 5 independent decisions rather than 60 (95% interval 3.4 to 9.2). On 114 real MCP tools with expert-written rules, the models' own manifests block 89% of attacks yet leave 9 of 15 catalogs open, as the author-effect model predicts and independence does not. Evaluations should report catalog vulnerability, the sink coverage of their tests, and an effective number of independent decisions alongside per-attack blocking.

items.summary: Modern commodity DPI systems are capable of analyzing packet sizes, directions, and timings to detect circumvention tools even when those tools use sophisticated obfuscation. The anti-censorship community has called for innovation in traffic shaping and built an ecosystem that facilitates the adoption of new shaping techniques. However, a fundamental gap is halting progress: \textit{what} should circumvention traffic look like? Past experience with traffic shaping has underscored that effective shaping must produce traffic that looks like legitimate Internet traffic while limiting the ability of censors to identify multiple proxies through shared fingerprints. In this paper, we use our access to large-scale real-world TLS traffic at a regional ISP to analyze approximately 12 million connections, finding that individual servers differ substantially from the broader TLS population and that traffic patterns vary across services. Combining these empirical observations with past experience with traffic shaping, we build CenShaper, which shapes each proxy's traffic to look like a selected TLS server. To reproduce these server-specific patterns, CenShaper trains a shared generative model using traffic from TLS connections to many servers and adapts it for each proxy using a small sample of recorded connections to its selected server. Our model evaluation shows that fingerprints learned from known proxies transfer poorly to proxies imitating previously unseen TLS services. In end-to-end testing, CenShaper reduces the detection rate of TLS-over-TLS fingerprinting from over 85\% to approximately 3\% at a 1\% false positive rate. Finally, we show how running CenShaper as a sidecar process simplifies integration with existing circumvention tools, making it a practical defense against increasingly powerful traffic analysis attacks.
items.title: CenShaper: Shaping Proxy Traffic for Censorship Circumvention

items.summary: Recent incidents involving agents bypassing sandboxing and network isolation have raised concerns about existing agent harnesses, prompting frontier labs such as OpenAI to reevaluate the security of their training platforms. Incident reviews show that determined agents can escape processes, containers, and VMs, or bypass their isolation through advanced side and covert channels. Follow-up audits also found that some agents concealed their actions by disabling monitoring and tampering with logs. We propose Airlock, an architecture that pairs each agent's VM with an Airlock VM, each running in a separate hardware-isolated Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). The Airlock VM fully mediates the agent's interactions with the outside world, including network and storage operations. We modify the firmware layer of Arm's Confidential Computing Architecture, Realm Management Monitor (RMM), and the kernels of both VMs so that the Airlock VM serves the agent VM's IO without involving the host. We adapt OpenShell, an agent runtime supporting sandboxing and governance policies, to this architecture. Airlock keeps network and filesystem policies, and credential protection effective even if the agent VM is fully compromised, and it removes the host from the agent's IO path, reducing opportunities for collusion and covert channels with the host. Finally, we extend the Airlock VM's capabilities to provide tamper-proof auditing of all agent operations, preserving forensic evidence even if the Airlock VM is compromised. We implement and evaluate Airlock on a Radxa development board. items.summary: Agent Skills has gained widespread adoption as an open standard for extending agent capabilities. To facilitate skill sharing, public skill hubs have grown in popularity and increasingly rely on automated security detectors to identify malicious skills at scale. Yet, the effectiveness and limitations of these detectors remain insufficiently understood. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study of four hub-adopted and two community-provided malicious skill detectors on 1477 agent skills from seven datasets. Our evaluation reveals that even the best-performing hub-adopted detector by overall F1, skill-scanner with Qwen3.6, still misses 4.9% of malicious skills and incorrectly flags 17.8% of benign skills. To understand these failures, we manually analyze detectors' findings and decision-making processes, identifying two recurring failure mechanisms. False positives often arise when detectors flag sensitive operations, such as credential access, without considering whether they serve the skill's legitimate purpose. Conversely, false negatives occur when detectors recognize malicious instructions or behaviors but underestimate their severity or dismiss valid findings during review, ultimately leaving malicious skills unblocked. Guided by this analysis, we refine the prompts of a state-of-the-art detector, skill-vetter, improving its mean F1 score in eight of nine evaluation settings, with gains of up to 22.7 percentage points. These results highlight gaps in existing skill-vetting practices and underscore the need for more robust and context-aware detection mechanisms.
items.title: Demystifying Detectors Guarding Agent Skill Hubs

items.summary: Functional (programmable) bootstrapping extends the bootstrapping operation of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to evaluate an arbitrary function while refreshing a ciphertext. This capability was a unique feature of scalar CGGI/DM cryptosystems for many years until it was recently added to the toolset of vectorized FHE schemes, with CKKS being the most promising option both in terms of throughput (amortized time) and functionality. Previous work showed that CKKS functional bootstrapping outperforms CGGI/DM functional bootstrapping in terms of throughput by two to three orders of magnitude, but still loses in latency on CPU by two to three orders of magnitude. We present an optimized GPU implementation of CKKS functional bootstrapping that closes the latency gap. Our implementation supports evaluating functions over both small integers (as in CGGI/DM) and real numbers (unique to CKKS), which we call discrete-CKKS and continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping, respectively.
items.title: High Throughput Meets Low Latency: CKKS Functional Bootstrapping on GPUs

The platforms set these rules, but vendors running programs on them bear the cost when a vulnerability goes unreported and gets exploited. items.summary: While frontier language models are becoming capable cybersecurity assistants, they also create a dual-use cyber risk: the same capabilities that help defenders identify and analyze vulnerabilities can similarly help attackers weaponize them. Existing cyber benchmarks measure either raw offensive capability or generic refusal behavior, overlooking the dual-use cyber assessment of preserving benign security utility while refusing assistance that materially advances misuse. We introduce CyberDualEval, a benchmark with 430 vulnerable tasks for measuring dual-use cyber risk in frontier language models. Each task is decomposed into three phases of increasing operationalization: security analysis, proof-of-concept generation, and exploit generation. To quantify the residual cyber risk, we annotate each task with a Task Weaponization Score that measures how much work remains to turn the resulting artifact into unauthorized cyber misuse. CyberDualEval assesses ten closed- and open-weight language models both on correct compliance and on task performance, developing four deterministic mechanisms for determining per-phase success on a large subset of the dataset. Our evaluation reveals that none of the existing frontier models effectively navigate helping with safe requests and refusing risky ones, characterized by being overly-cautious. On the other hand, recent open-weight models rarely refuse and demonstrate strong validated accuracy on risky requests.
items.title: CyberDualEval: Measuring Dual-Use Cyber Risks in Frontier Language Models

items.summary: Remote timing attacks exploit variations in response times to infer sensitive information about remote systems. Their effectiveness, however, is often limited by the difficulty of accurately modeling the stochastic nature of server-side response times, taking into account the intrinsic variability of the service time of a request and the impact of varying workloads on the observed response times. In this article, we propose a new stochastic framework for remote timing attacks based on queuing models and Bayesian statistics. We assume that the attacker knows the service time distributions of two classes of requests and that the information leakage occurs when a malicious observer can distinguish with high probability the class based on the observed response times in the presence of noise induced by exogenous workload. Our experimental evaluation on popular websites demonstrates the practical viability of the approach: our attack outperforms formal techniques based on deterministic service times and existing empirical techniques, while requiring less tuning and fewer hyper-parameters compared to previous formal approaches. Overall, our results show that principled stochastic modeling can provide a solid foundation for building more effective remote timing attacks under realistic network and workload conditions.

items.summary: A central challenge in Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) is the selection of ciphertext moduli, which depends on accurately estimating noise growth during homomorphic evaluation. Choosing excessively large moduli reduces the efficiency and scalability of the scheme, whereas underestimating noise can result in decryption failures and potential security vulnerabilities. Average-case analyses have provided promising probabilistic estimates of noise growth in practical FHE computations. However, recent studies indicate that reliable estimates must account for dependencies among ciphertext errors, as neglecting these correlations can systematically underestimate noise. This work presents the first average-case analysis for the BGV scheme that accounts for both correlations induced by secret/public keys and ciphertext dependencies. We propose new variance estimates for the noise coefficients in homomorphic additions and multiplications involving dependent ciphertexts, and extend our framework to the homomorphic evaluation of polynomial functions, which is widely employed in FHE applications. Our theoretical estimates closely align with experimental observations, exhibiting discrepancies smaller than 1.2 bits. Finally, these estimates are adopted to choose the initial BGV parameters, leading to significantly smaller ciphertext moduli compared to those currently adopted in widely used FHE libraries, thus improving the efficiency of the scheme. Compared to OpenFHE, we obtain an average reduction of about 11.5% in the ciphertext modulus size, while relative to HElib, we reduce the ratio between consecutive moduli up to 23 bits per level in practical settings.
items.title: From Dependent Ciphertexts to Sharp Bounds for Polynomial Evaluation in BGV

items.summary: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.
items.title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?

items.summary: Mirror-based LiDAR attacks passively redirect automotive LiDAR's beams to create phantom objects in the vehicle perception. Recent work has demonstrated that these attacks may cause vehicles to brake for a phantom where nothing stands. Every phantom return is a genuine time-of-flight measurement, so current spoofing defenses are not able to differentiate phantoms from real objects. We present MirrorGuard, a physics-informed defense that identifies and removes mirror-induced phantom returns before they affect downstream perception. MirrorGuard tests three consequences of the reflected path. Every phantom bearing crosses the mirror's finite aperture, its opaque surface blocks any direct return beyond it, and the two reflections off the mirror dim the phantom. MirrorGuard identifies a phantom by these cues over multiple scans and removes the reflected beams before it reaches any detector or occupancy grid. On real-world recordings of this attack, MirrorGuard removes 96.31% of the phantom's returns at 98.30% precision, with 99.99% of non-phantom returns untouched. In a closed loop with the CARLA driving simulator and the open-source stack (Autoware), a vehicle without the defense halts for an obstacle that is not present and a following car crashes into its rear. With MirrorGuard, no vehicle produces a halt or a crash. MirrorGuard runs at 59 ms mean per scan on a CPU and is a software-only solution that does not require new hardware or environmental training.
items.title: MirrorGuard: Defending LiDAR Perception against Passive Mirror Attacks

Evaluating an agent only on whether its goal exists can hide harmful recovery actions: auditing 12 supplied traces changes apparent completion from 10/12 to 8/12. In 3,456 model episodes, the original task wording produces only 39/576 valid recoveries when the initial write is absent; a combined clarification produces 576/576. Definition alone yields 276/288 valid recoveries; recipe alone yields 288/288. For Luna, malicious text is associated with 11.1 percentage points fewer valid recoveries under both original and definition-only wording, an availability signal limited by shared tasks and templates. The stronger attacks produce no attempted unauthorized or changed-key action and no unsafe effect. A trajectory audit finds six original-key retries after observing pending status: five denied and one deduplicated. Bounded checks distinguish atomic key enforcement from a delayed-commit race; stale negative reads also invalidate the evidence gate. A separate Claude Code program adds 720 successful episodes: 288 under the original attacks and 432 stronger-attack calibration episodes across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 5.5, with no observed proposal or effect deviations. items.summary: We give polynomial-time algorithms for Gaussian multi-sampling under approximate $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differential privacy, with optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors. Our main construction uses $\widetilde{O}(m+d\sqrt{m}/\varepsilon)$ independent input samples from a $d$-dimensional Gaussian $P$ with unknown mean and covariance to generate $m$ exactly independent outputs. Their joint distribution is $α$-close in total variation to $P^{\otimes m}$. Our lower bounds hold even for dependent outputs under the same joint accuracy guarantee, showing that exact independence incurs no additional sample cost beyond logarithmic factors. The single-sampler of Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis [COLT 2025] uses $\widetilde{O}(d/\varepsilon)$ input samples. Running it on a separate input dataset for each of $m$ outputs therefore costs $\widetilde{O}(md/\varepsilon)$ in total. Our construction reduces this dimension-dependent sample cost from linear to square-root dependence on the number of outputs. Our approach builds on the stable weighted statistics of Brown, Hopkins, and Smith [COLT 2023], also used for Gaussian single-sampling by Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis. To control privacy loss when the entire batch shares these statistics, we compare the joint output densities and obtain a privacy bound that scales with the square root of the batch size. The stability step downweights influential records and can reject the entire batch. Both actions can make the outputs dependent. Our correction restores exact independence while preserving differential privacy and joint accuracy.
items.title: Optimal Private Gaussian Multi-sampling

items.summary: We design a lightweight authentication and key agreement protocol for Internet of Drones (IoD) environments that simultaneously provides post-quantum security, hardware-rooted trust, and resistance against machine-learning-based Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) modeling attacks. Existing PUF-based authentication schemes for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer protection against cloning and physical capture, but generally lack resistance against quantum adversaries. Conversely, recent post-quantum UAV authentication protocols provide quantum-resistant key establishment, yet do not incorporate hardware-bound authentication mechanisms and therefore remain vulnerable to device cloning and physical compromise. To address these limitations, we integrate CRYSTALS-Kyber, dynamic challenge scrambling (DCS), fuzzy extractors, and PUF-based identity binding into a unified framework. The resulting protocol enables anonymous authentication, forward secrecy, resistance to physical capture and replay attacks, and secure drone-to-drone communication, while maintaining suitability for resource-constrained UAV platforms. We provide a formal security analysis of the proposed scheme under the real-or-random model, a ProVerif-based formal verification, an informal analysis of its effectiveness against various attacks, and a performance evaluation of the proposed scheme through communication, computation, and storage cost analyses, which show its advantages over state-of-the-art architectures.
items.title: Quantum-Resilient, PUF-Based, and Anonymity-Preserving Authentication and Key Agreement Scheme for UAV Networks

items.summary: Recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS), voice conversion (VC), and AI-driven speech synthesis enable adversaries to convincingly impersonate trusted individuals during phone calls. Existing defenses often rely on offline analysis, degrade under telephony distortions, or remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks. To address these limitations, we present Ultrasound Watermark, a real-time, smartphone-native framework that protects live calls by binding speech to the caller's physical articulatory motion through acoustic watermarking. During a call, the smartphone emits ultrasonic signals and captures reflections from facial articulatory movements using only its built-in speaker and microphone. Ultrasound Watermark extracts motion features from these reflections and fuses them with outgoing speech to generate a dynamic watermark. Because the ultrasonic measurements are physically and temporally coupled with speech production, they are difficult to spoof without the underlying articulatory motion. A synchronized generator-detector architecture enforces cross-modal speech-motion consistency against replay, synthesized speech, and articulation-mimicking attacks. Ultrasound Watermark operates continuously with less than 200 ms latency overhead and requires no additional hardware. We implement Ultrasound Watermark on iOS and Android and evaluate it using over 2.5 hours of synchronized speech-ultrasound recordings from 22 speakers across eight smartphones and four real-world environments. items.summary: The hockey-stick divergence is a fundamental distinguishability measure in quantum information theory. It characterizes quantum differential privacy and determines the optimal error probability of binary quantum hypothesis testing with arbitrary priors. We study how it behaves on tensor-product states. To this end, we consider the noncommutative minimum $m(A,B):=(\mathrm{Tr}[A]+\mathrm{Tr}[B]-\|A-B\|_1)/2$ of positive semidefinite operators, which reduces to $\sum_x\min\{a_x,b_x\}$ when $A$ and $B$ commute, and we prove that it is super-multiplicative, i.e., $m(A\otimes C,B\otimes D)\ge m(A,B)\,m(C,D)$. As a consequence, we establish a sub-additivity property of the hockey-stick divergence on product states, in which the parameters of the individual systems are multiplied, and no additional prefactor appears. We show that this bound is tight, also for noncommuting states, and that it is strict for faithful states whenever at least two of the divergences are positive. Using this, we obtain sub-additivity of the Datta-Leditzky divergences, a parallel composition theorem for quantum differentially private channels under product neighboring inputs with at most linear degradation of the privacy parameters, and a sharp sub-additivity property of the hypothesis-testing relative entropy normalized by the acceptance probability. Finally, we apply the same tools to symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing. We determine the exact prefactor of the quantum Chernoff bound for every pair of noncommuting states satisfying mild conditions including a nonlattice condition and, under a quantitative version of this condition, the full asymptotic expansion to every fixed order in $1/n$, with explicitly computable coefficients. As a consequence, we determine the sample complexity of symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing up to one sample, as the error probability tends to zero.
items.title: Super-Multiplicativity of the Noncommutative Minimum and Applications to Quantum Privacy and Hypothesis Testing

items.summary: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.
items.title: EnvTrap: Revealing the Environment-Only Attack Surface in Embodied AI via Consequence-Blind Action Execution

items.summary: Frontier AI governance agreements require compute verification techniques that allow an external observer to confirm that a hardware operator does not run prohibited workloads. Off-chip, analogue hardware signals, such as power draw, have been proposed as a potential information channel for compute verification. Such signals can be measured externally, without the operator's cooperation. We show that the supply current drawn by a GPU can be used to verify the work declared by the GPU operator, without requiring examples of prohibited workloads or evasion strategies. We record 23.4 h of GPU current with a Rogowski coil under idle, training and inference workloads. We consider five evasion strategies an operator might use to disguise prohibited training. We show that a one-class model fitted to the current draw of permitted, declared work (idle and inference) flags at least 99.9% of windows of prohibited training, including training hidden by the five evasion strategies. As a continuous monitor across successive windows, it detects all 188 episodes of prohibited training hidden by time-sharing with declared inference, with a median delay of 3.0 s, and raises one alarm in 8.8 h of declared work. Incomplete or corrupt recordings of the declared work can undermine verification. An incomplete recording fails loudly; with idle missing, the monitor is in alarm for 99.97% of declared idle. A corrupt recording can fail silently; if the operator runs training during the recording, the monitor can miss hidden training while raising no alarm on declared work. These results suggest that operator declarations together with external analogue sensing might offer a practical route to compute verification.
items.title: Verifying Declared AI Workloads from GPU Supply Current

items.summary: Harnesses secure Computer-Using Agents by enforcing security constraints and defending against prompt injection attacks. However, we find that two core security mechanisms of agent harnesses remain vulnerable. First, consistency checking prevents agents from deviating from legitimate user objectives, while attackers can bypass it by embedding malicious actions that appear logically consistent with legitimate task execution. Second, risk auditing proactively examines high-risk operations. Yet, the auditing process itself would introduce additional exploitable actions that violate security boundaries. To evaluate above defects we found, we propose Conartist, a cascaded adaptive prompt injection framework comprising two progressive stages. First, Conartist employs a goal-pollution strategy to establish deceptive causal dependencies between legitimate user objectives and malicious operations, progressively embedding attack steps into legitimate task workflows. However, these task-coupled attacks remain susceptible to risk auditing. To address this limitation, Conartist further analyzes security-auditing feedback from controlled attack exploration to identify exploitable auditing patterns. Conartist then adaptively refines its deception strategies to either avoid triggering risk auditing or induce additional high-risk operations. Extensive experiments across five backbone models demonstrate the effectiveness of Conartist, achieving attack success rates of 32.12% on 576-instance tool use benchmark and 66.67% in the Reddit GUI benchmark, outperforming the SOTA attack by 14.41 and 29.17, respectively. By analyzing one of the most popular Agent, Openclaw, we furthermore concluded seven realistic exploitable attack patterns, which reveals that security mechanisms designed to prevent malicious actions can themselves be manipulated to facilitate attacks.
items.title: Conartist: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Computer-Using Agents against Multi-Step Prompt Injection

items.summary: Anomaly-based malicious traffic detection learns decision boundaries for normal behavior and identifies deviations as anomalies. However, normal behavior varies across networks and changes dynamically, limiting adaptability and increasing retraining costs. Despite this variability, our measurements show that clients accessing the same service exhibit consistent flow structures and interaction patterns, since each service provides specific functionality. We therefore construct service-specific decision boundaries. However, variations in personalized requests make it difficult to construct stable boundaries. To address this challenge, we propose IDSMorph, a self-adaptive malicious traffic detection system that learns consistency-guided embeddings through two key designs: (1) a flow structure consistency builder, which constructs contrastive samples capturing consistent embeddings within services; and (2) a service interaction consistency builder, which captures local structural consistency among different clients and global behavioral consistency among clients accessing that service. IDSMorph constructs dynamic decision boundaries from the majority of similar embeddings within each service and dynamically updates them through a differencing algorithm that mitigates the transient traffic shifts within short observation windows. Experiments show that IDSMorph's detection F1 score decreases by no more than 0.12 points across network environments, compared with an average decrease of 55.43 points for prior methods. In real-world deployment with red-team operators independently choosing attack strategies and timing, IDSMorph achieves an F1 score 46.81 points higher than other methods.
items.title: IDSMorph: Self-Adaptive Malicious Traffic Detection through Consistency-Guided Dynamic Decision Boundaries

We pack $128$ syndrome bits into one $16$-byte ulonglong2 without left-triple indices (lossless for $mt \le 145$, and extended to $mt \le 192$ via truncated range pre-filtering), share $G \in \{4, 8\}$ cooperative tables inside GPU L2 cache, batch $64G$ random systematic reductions per launch, and widen the shortening prefix $n'$ to cut modeled GPU-hours by $34\%\text{-}47\%$. Across five Track-2 challenges ($mt = 108 \to 153$), every recovered private key passes both the official SageMath checker and a standalone pure-Python verifier. Eight Modal L40S GPUs solve TII-228 ($mt=126$) in $18.9\text{ min}$ ($2.15$ GPU-hours, $3.0\times$ faster in wall-clock than MiniMax's EPYC cluster). We further recover keys for the previously undocumented challenges TII-237 ($mt=135$, $22.1$ L4 GPU-hours), TII-235 ($mt=144$, $39.62$ L40S GPU-hours, $17.97\text{ s}$ lift), and TII-185 ($mt=153$, $140.4$ L40S + $\approx 60$ L4 GPU-hours, $39.01\text{ s}$ lift). items.summary: We propose a new coding-theoretic problem motivated by censorship resistance. Is it possible to intertwine many pieces of data by encoding them jointly in a way that makes it impossible to remove any single piece without destroying many others as well? In particular, we want to encode $k$ data components $(m_1,\ldots, m_k)$ into a codeword $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ with the following properties: 1. Local recovery: every data component can be recovered (in the absence of erasures or errors) by reading at most $\ell$ correct codeword symbols. 2. Unshardability: if an adversary erases some arbitrary subset of the codeword symbols, the remaining codeword symbols either uniquely determine all $k$ data components, or there are at least $s$ data components that cannot be determined. We call such codes $(\ell, s)$-unshardable. Intuitively, such codes prevent an adversary from selectively censoring individual pieces of data by erasing codeword symbols, without destroying large amounts of other data as collateral damage. We show that codes whose generator matrix has certain superregularity properties are unshardable. Using this connection, we construct linear codes that are $(\ell, s)$-unshardable with $s = (1-\varepsilon)k$ and locality $\ell = O_\varepsilon(1)$. We also show that linear unshardable codes are subject to the lower bound $s \leq k - k/\ell + 1$. Finally, we consider a strengthening of local recovery to also require local decodability from some constant fraction of erasures or even errors. With the help of AI tools, we achieve the above notion by showing that any Locally Decodable Code (LDC) can be converted into one that is unshardable while preserving locality via a certain careful change of basis over an appropriate extension field.

A quirk in how the .NET Framework loads a program file let a local attacker run untrusted code past two separate protections on Windows built to block it, Google Project Zero researcher James Forshaw showed in a write-up published yesterday.

The same loading behavior bypassed Oracle VirtualBox's process hardening on Windows hosts, tracked as CVE-2026-87268, and Windows code integrity, tracked
items.title: Google Researcher Shows How a Single Bit Change in .NET Files Bypassed Windows Code Integrity

items.summary:
Strong::Random versions through 0.96 for Perl allow every later rand output to be predicted from three earlier ones.

The generator keeps its state in a single number. Each call multiplies the state by a factor derived from it, and the returned digits encode that factor, so three consecutive outputs determine the state however the generator was seeded. Outputs are also biased: the first digit after the decimal point is never zero, so rand(256) never returns 1 to 24.

An attacker who sees three consecutive outputs can predict the tokens, passwords or key bytes that the same object later issues to other users.

items.summary:
MCUboot's Espressif port omits zeroization of two sensitive stack buffers in boot/espressif/hal/src/flash_encrypt.c. In check_and_generate_encryption_keys(), the freshly generated XTS-AES flash-encryption key is held in the stack array keys[BLOCKS_NEEDED][32] (flash_encrypt.c:216), written to eFuse via esp_efuse_write_keys(), and the function returns (flash_encrypt.c:243) without scrubbing it. In esp_flash_encrypt_region(), the plaintext flash sector buffer buf (flash_encrypt.c:454) retains the last sector's cleartext at both the success and flash_failed returns. Neither path performs a memset/bzero/mbedtls_platform_zeroize, even though the same port already does bzero for key digests in boot/espressif/hal/src/secure_boot.c.

The affected code runs only on the Espressif port with CONFIG_SECURE_FLASH_ENC_ENABLED, and only during the one-time first-boot provisioning pass when flash encryption is not yet enabled (boot/espressif/main.c); on subsequent boots the buffers are never created. Recovering the residue requires an out-of-band stack/RAM-disclosure primitive — JTAG/debug halt, UART ROM download, a core/crash dump, or a warm-boot RAM scrape — captured during that single provisioning boot. Under the recommended CONFIG_SECURE_FLASH_ENCRYPTION_MODE_RELEASE plus secure boot, those channels are fused off and no exposure exists.

The practical impact is a low-severity, defense-in-depth hardening gap: a flash-encryption key (and last plaintext sector) may linger in bootloader stack memory. Because the eFuse key block is burned read+write-protected, the transient stack copy is the only readable copy, and only during one boot; in a development build where a disclosure channel is open, an attacker with that capability can usually already read the still-plaintext flash directly, so the marginal confidentiality gain is small. Confirming real-world recovery depends on a specific SoC/debug configuration not exercisable from source alone.

items.summary:
MCUboot's PSA-crypto ECDSA adapter parses the RFC 5480 DER signature with parse_signature_from_rfc5480_encoding() in boot/bootutil/include/bootutil/crypto/ecdsa.h, which takes no length argument. bootutil_ecdsa_verify() explicitly discards the signature length ((void)slen;) and the parser walks the encoding using length bytes read from the buffer itself (r_len = sig[3], then a derived s_len), with no check that those offsets stay within the supplied signature. Because this parsing runs before psa_verify_hash(), a malformed signature triggers the read whether or not the signature is valid.

In bootutil_img_validate() (boot/bootutil/src/image_validate.c:404) the ECDSA signature TLV is gated only by len > sizeof(buf), since EXPECTED_SIG_LEN() is the constant 1 for ECDSA; len is attacker-controlled in the range 0..128 and is copied into the 128-byte stack buffer buf. With a crafted r_len (e.g. sig[3] = 255) the parser's memcpy reads roughly 130+ bytes past the end of buf, an out-of-bounds read of adjacent stack memory. Reaching the signature case only requires a key TLV that matches a trusted public key (public material), so the path is effectively pre-authentication.

The defect is gated to the PSA crypto backend (MCUBOOT_USE_PSA_CRYPTO) with MCUBOOT_SIGN_EC256/MCUBOOT_SIGN_EC384 (and MCUBOOT_SIGN_EC384 always builds with PSA); the in-tree CC310, TinyCrypt, and mbedTLS adapters use different decoders and are not affected. This is not a signature bypass: the over-read bytes feed a verification that fails closed and are never returned to the attacker, so there is no information leak. The impact is bounded to a possible fault/denial-of-service on memory layouts where the read crosses an unmapped region; on typical flat-memory MCUs it reads adjacent RAM without faulting.
This vulnerability was reported independently twice: by NVIDIA Project Vanessa on 2026-06-22, and by Kai Phan (@kaimandalic) on 2026-07-19 as GHSA-r44p-8v6p-hqv4, which is closed as a duplicate of this advisory. Both original reports are reproduced in full below. The second report additionally observes that bootutil_ecdsa_parse_public_key() discards its end pointer ((void)end;, ecdsa.h:446). That observation is correct, but it is not part of this vulnerability and is not counted in the severity: the buffer it parses is bootutil_keys[key_id].key, the compiled-in trusted key store (image_ecdsa.c:54-55), so no attacker-controlled data reaches that parse. It is a robustness gap on the same code path and should be closed alongside the signature-parser fix. Note also that the second report's proof-of-concept models the signature buffer as an 8-byte heap allocation and therefore reports a heap overflow; in MCUboot the buffer is the 128-byte stack array buf, gated by len > sizeof(buf), so the real over-read is of adjacent stack memory.

items.summary:
The Cypress/PSoC6 flash-map backend in boot/cypress/cy_flash_pal/cy_flash_map.c guards every flash access with assert() against the wrong struct field. flash_area_read(), flash_area_write(), and flash_area_erase() check assert(off < fa->fa_off) and assert(off + len < fa->fa_off), comparing the area-relative off against the partition's absolute base address fa->fa_off instead of its length fa->fa_size. Because fa_off is a large absolute address, realistic out-of-partition offsets pass the check even in a debug build, and under NDEBUG the asserts are removed entirely. The access then proceeds as memcpy() (or a flash row op) at fa->fa_off + off with no enforcement.

The MCUboot core does not bound image-region offsets itself; it relies on flash_area_read() returning an error. During pre-authentication image validation, bootutil_img_hash() in boot/bootutil/src/bootutil_img_hash.c loops over ih_hdr_size + ih_img_size + ih_protect_tlv_size — all attacker-controlled header fields of the still-unverified update image — calling flash_area_read(), and the TLV iterator in boot/bootutil/src/tlv.c reads attacker-derived offsets the same way. An attacker who can stage a crafted image in the secondary/update slot (via OTA, DFU, or serial recovery, depending on the product) declares an oversized ih_img_size, causing reads far past the partition. A correct backend would reject these and fail validation cleanly; the Cypress backend does not.

The out-of-bounds access is in the source address of the copy — the destination buffer is correctly sized — so there is no memory corruption, no information disclosure to the attacker (the data is only folded into a hash that still fails the signature check), and no authentication bypass. The realistic impact is a bus fault or hang when the computed absolute address lands on an unmapped or peripheral region of the PSoC6 address map: the bootloader crashes instead of rejecting the bad image, an availability (denial-of-service) impact. The defect is specific to the Cypress/PSoC6 port; mainline Zephyr/sim/mynewt backends are unaffected. The identical broken guard in the write/erase primitives is a latent out-of-bounds-write gap, but no attacker-controlled out-of-bounds offset was found to reach those (serial-recovery uploads are bounded by the core), so the reachable memory-safety bug is the out-of-bounds read.

items.recommended_action: 建议根据原文自行评估
items.summary:
When MCUboot resumes an interrupted image swap it takes the number of bytes to move straight from the flash-resident status trailer. In boot_swap_image() (boot/bootutil/src/loader.c) the fresh-swap branch recomputes copy_size from the image headers and is bounded — swap_run() in boot/bootutil/src/swap_move.c carries an explicit "not enough free space" check (last_idx >= first_trailer_idx) — but that check runs only inside if (boot_status_is_reset(bs)). On the resume branch the code instead does boot_read_swap_size(fap, &bs->swap_size); copy_size = bs->swap_size; and passes the value to swap_run() with no re-derivation and no bound.

swap_run() turns that byte count into a sector index by summing sector sizes until it reaches the count, with no ceiling on the real sector count: find_last_idx() in swap_move.c and swap_offset.c, and find_last_sector_idx() in swap_scratch.c, are all while (1) loops. The resulting index is fed to boot_img_sector_off() / boot_img_sector_size() (boot/bootutil/src/bootutil_priv.h), which index the fixed BOOT_MAX_IMG_SECTORS sectors[] arrays with no bounds check. Past num_sectors the loop reads zero-initialised — and past BOOT_MAX_IMG_SECTORS, adjacent-struct — entries; a sector size of 0 makes the loop never terminate, and a bogus computed offset is handed to boot_erase_region() / boot_copy_region() as an out-of-bounds flash erase or copy.

MCUboot itself only ever writes a validated, slot-bounded swap_size (swap_misc.c, fixup_revert()), so reaching the defect requires writing the trailer from outside. Serial recovery provides exactly that: an upload writes attacker bytes contiguously from offset 0 of the primary slot (boot/boot_serial/src/boot_serial.c, via flash_area_id_from_multi_image_slot()), bounded only by img_size <= area_size, so it controls the whole trailer — magic, swap_info, op/idx/state and swap_size. The resume gate boot_status_is_reset() keys solely on those op/idx/state fields, and boot_find_status() explicitly trusts valid magic as implying valid metadata. A forged in-progress status with an oversized swap_size therefore drives the unbounded walk during swap setup — before the primary image's signature is validated, and serial recovery is unauthenticated by design.

The outcome is an out-of-bounds flash erase or copy, or a non-terminating loop, inside the bootloader: an unbootable or bricked device, with the possibility of bootloader memory corruption. That exceeds what serial recovery is designed to grant, which is only the ability to stage an image that must still pass signature verification.

Exposure requires a swap-based update backend — MCUBOOT_SWAP_USING_MOVE (the default for swap builds), MCUBOOT_SWAP_USING_SCRATCH or MCUBOOT_SWAP_USING_OFFSET; overwrite-only, direct-XIP and RAM-load builds are unaffected — together with MCUBOOT_SERIAL_RECOVERY. Without serial recovery the path is only reachable by an attacker who can already write flash directly, which is outside the threat model.

The fix is to treat the trailer's swap_size as untrusted: reject or clamp it in boot_swap_image() before it becomes copy_size, bounding it by the primary slot's usable image area (sector count x sector size, excluding the trailer) rather than the raw flash_area_get_size(), and aborting recovery with a non-zero error on overflow. The same guard should cover the independent boot_read_swap_size() reads in each backend's boot_read_image_header().

items.summary: Inscriptis is a Python library for converting HTML to text. From 2.0.0 until 2.7.6, when the parent is block-level, table_end_handler() in model/tag/table_tag.py writes each sibling table through HtmlElement.write_verbatim_text() in model/html_element.py; Canvas.open_block() leaves the parent padding_inline prefix on the stack, Canvas.close_block() does not remove it, and only Canvas.close_tag() calls prefix.remove_last_prefix(). Each following sibling table therefore carries forward accumulated indentation, making get_text() output grow quadratically and allowing small attacker-controlled HTML to exhaust memory in applications converting it without authentication or user interaction. This issue is fixed in 2.7.6.

In Apache Karaf, the default command ACL configuration for the feature scope (etc/org.apache.karaf.command.acl.feature.cfg, defined in assemblies/features/standard/src/main/feature/feature.xml and the child-instance template instance/src/main/resources/org/apache/karaf/instance/resources/etc/org.apache.karaf.command.acl.feature.cfg) restricts feature:install, feature:uninstall, feature:start, and feature:stop to users with the admin role, while leaving feature:requirement-add and feature:requirement-remove without ACL entries.


Because Karaf's command guard (SecuredSessionFactoryImpl) allows commands with no matching ACL rule (NO_MATCH) to execute, an authenticated SSH user holding only the ssh and viewer roles can execute feature:requirement-add bundle:<uri> (or feature:<name>). RequirementAdd forwards the requirement directly to FeatureService.addRequirements(), causing the resolver to download, install, and start an arbitrary bundle with the Karaf JVM process's full authority, bypassing the admin-only restrictions on feature:install and bundle:install. Similarly, feature:requirement-remove allows removing provisioning requirements and uninstalling features/bundles.

MitigationUsers are recommended to upgrade to Apache Karaf 4.4.13 or 4.5.0.




For existing deployments or upgrades that preserve existing files in etc/, add the following rules to etc/org.apache.karaf.command.acl.feature.cfg (and any child instance etc/org.apache.karaf.command.acl.feature.cfg files):




requirement-add = admin 

requirement-remove = admin

The shell command ACL for the feature scope (etc/org.apache.karaf.command.acl.feature.cfg) restricts feature:install, feature:uninstall, feature:start and feature:stop to the admin role, but had no entry for feature:requirement-add or feature:requirement-remove.

The provisioning resolver turns a requirement into the same install/start (or uninstall) action as feature:install / feature:uninstall: a bundle: requirement causes an arbitrary bundle to be downloaded and started, and a feature: requirement installs that feature. This is the same class of issue as the feature:repo-add -i / feature:repo-remove -u bypass, on sibling commands not covered by that earlier fix.Mitigation:Upgrade to Apache Karaf 4.4.12 or 4.5.0 (or later), which restrict feature:requirement-add and feature:requirement-remove to the admin role.

As an interim workaround on affected versions, add the following two lines to etc/org.apache.karaf.command.acl.feature.cfg; the change is picked up at runtime without a restart:

requirement-add = admin

requirement-remove = admin

items.summary:
Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability in lasp-lang partisan allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to abort the Erlang VM of a node via Excessive Allocation. partisan_peer_service_server:handle_info/2 decodes every frame that arrives on the peer listener with binary_to_term/1, without the safe option, before handle_inbound/2 interprets the message and before any peer authentication takes place. TLS is off by default and the listener accepts connections from any host, so one frame that names more atoms than the atom table holds aborts the VM. partisan_peer_service_client:handle_info/2 decodes frames from the server side of a connection the same way.

The decode also materializes funs, ports and references the frame encodes and inflates compressed terms. The demonstrated impact is denial of service. partisan does not invoke decoded funs, so code execution was not shown.

This issue affects partisan: from 3.0.0 before 6.4.0.

The vulnerability occurs while parsing an Authorization or WWW-Authenticate header that uses Digest authentication. Specially crafted whitespace placement around a parameter's terminator can cause an internal length calculation to underflow, leading to a crash of the process parsing the header. On an RTSP server this can be triggered by a remote, unauthenticated attacker sending a single malformed request when the server has authentication enabled; the same flaw can also be triggered against an RTSP client by a malicious or compromised RTSP server. Successful exploitation results in a denial of service (application crash) and has no confirmed impact on confidentiality or integrity.

items.summary:
An algorithmic complexity flaw exists in libsoup's HTTP Range header processing that persists after the CVE-2025-32907 fix.

CVE-2025-32907 addressed memory amplification when a client repeated the same range many times in a single Range header. Commit 9bb92f7a corrected merge correctness in soup_message_headers_get_ranges_internal() in libsoup/soup-message-headers.c, but the coalescing loop still removes merged ranges using g_array_remove_index() for each coalesced element. Because GArray is contiguous, each mid-array removal performs an O(N) memmove. When many identical satisfiable ranges are supplied (for example bytes=0-0 repeated thousands of times), the loop performs O(N²) work coalescing them into a single range.

The vulnerable path is reachable server-side from handle_partial_get() in libsoup/server/http1/soup-server-message-io-http1.c when a SoupServer handler returns HTTP 200 with a non-empty body. No authentication is required. The number of ranges is bounded only by the maximum request header size (~100 KiB), allowing roughly 25,000 ranges per request. Reporter measurements on libsoup HEAD containing the CVE-2025-32907 fix show ~90 ms single-core CPU per such request at the wire maximum, blocking the server's event loop for that duration.

This is a CPU exhaustion / availability issue only. No memory corruption or information disclosure occurs.

Affected: libsoup versions containing the CVE-2025-32907 fix but not merge request !550.
Fixed upstream: MR !550 merged 2026-08-20, replacing per-element removal with O(N) in-place compaction and rejecting Range headers requesting more than 200 ranges.
Upstream report: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/libsoup/-/issues/538
Related: CVE-2025-32907

items.summary:
Issue summary: Calling EVP_EncodeBlock() with an input length close to INT_MAX
may overflow the calculation of the encoded output size and write past the end
of the caller-supplied output buffer.

Impact summary: No path by which an attacker can trigger this has been
identified. An application that passes an input length near INT_MAX to
EVP_EncodeBlock() could suffer a heap buffer overflow, crashing or corrupting
its own memory, but it must itself supply such a length.

CWE: CWE-190: Integer Overflow or Wraparound

Description: EVP_EncodeBlock() base64-encodes a buffer of a caller-supplied
length into an output buffer that the caller allocates. The caller is expected
to reserve 4*((len+2)/3)+1 bytes. For input lengths close to INT_MAX, the
arithmetic that computes the encoded length overflows a signed integer, so the
function writes more data than the documented output size. The result is a
heap buffer overflow in the calling process.

Reaching this requires an application to pass an input length near INT_MAX to
EVP_EncodeBlock(). OpenSSL's TLS, QUIC and CMS implementations never encode
buffers of that size, and the command line tools cannot practically be made to
do so: the limits on reading a proxy password from a file and on bignum sizes
prevent it. An application that accepts an attacker-controlled length and
forwards it to EVP_EncodeBlock() without its own bound check is exposed.

The severity is Low because no attacker-controlled path to the overflow is
known. The caller must already hold a buffer of about two gigabytes before the
defect can be reached.

FIPS impact: no
The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

items.summary: Lookyloo is a web-based URL capture and analysis platform. Prior to the fix, the authorization mechanism for private captures (seed-based access control) was not consistently enforced at the data access layer. The capture_cache method and numerous internal methods (get_info, get_meta, get_statistics, get_modules_responses, get_data, get_video, get_screenshot, get_har, get_cookies, get_storage_state, get_frames, get_console_messages, get_capture, get_ressource, misp_export, lacus_export, ai_export, comparator functions, and others) could be invoked with only a capture UUID without validating the required seed token. This meant that API endpoints and internal code paths that called these methods directly could return private capture data to unauthenticated users or users lacking the correct seed. The before_request hook in the web interface provided a partial check, but the underlying data layer did not enforce it, creating an inconsistent authorization boundary. An attacker who knew or guessed a private capture UUID could potentially access sensitive data including rendered screenshots, HAR files, downloaded files, cookies, storage state, console messages, and MISP exports through various REST API endpoints and web routes. The fix introduces a LookylooPrivateCapture exception raised at the cache layer when a private capture is accessed without a valid seed, refactors the API to pass CaptureCache objects (already validated) rather than raw UUIDs, and ensures all web and API endpoints propagate the session-known seed or admin status to the data access layer. The issue is fixed in version 3.1.14.

Elastic Agent is also affected when the Network Packet Capture integration monitors Cassandra traffic, because it uses the same protocol decoder.

items.recommended_action: 建议根据原文自行评估
items.summary: Pion DTLS is a Go implementation of Datagram Transport Layer Security. From 2.1.4 until 3.1.13, the handshake cache copied and retained submitted messages without deduplicating entries, limiting the entry count, limiting total payload bytes, or stopping new insertions after handshake completion. A remote peer able to deliver suitable DTLS traffic can grow the cache through incoming handshake messages and repeated caching of outgoing retransmissions for the lifetime of the connection. The fragment reassembly buffer's separate size limit does not prevent this issue because completed messages are retained in the append-only handshake cache. Unbounded cache growth can exhaust application memory and cause a denial of service. The issue is fixed in version 3.1.13.

From 2.0.0 until 3.1.13, peer certificates were parsed and their RSA public keys were passed to handshake signature and certificate-chain verification without an explicit modulus-size limit. A remote peer can provide a certificate with an unusually large attacker-chosen RSA modulus and an invalid signature; no corresponding private key or valid handshake signature is required to trigger the expensive operation. An RSA verification path must execute. A local ECDSA certificate does not prevent the peer from presenting an RSA certificate, and WebRTC deployments can be affected. Repeated or concurrent malicious handshakes can consume substantial CPU resources, delay legitimate connections, and reduce service availability. The issue is fixed in version 3.1.13.

items.summary: An attacker who controls the registry, a mirror, or the network path to it may be able to serve arbitrary image content in response to a pull by digest, so that a user runs an image other than the one they pinned. The fix compares the returned digest to the pinned digest and fails the pull on a mismatch. Tag pulls are exempt, because a tag is mutable by design. The fix also verifies the hash of manifests and blobs when they are fetched. This vulnerability is addressed in container version 1.6.0 and containerization version 0.52.1.

items.summary:
Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability in ash-project ash allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code or inject SQL through a forged keyset pagination cursor.

Ash.Page.Keyset.filter/4 in lib/ash/page/keyset.ex decodes the client-supplied page[:after] or page[:before] cursor from Erlang external term format and rejects decoded expressions with Ash.Expr.expr?/1. That check does not examine the fields of a struct. The cast of each value against the type of its sort field accepts structs for the :ci_string, :map, :struct and :term types. A struct in the cursor value for such a sort field therefore reaches the data layer. With AshPostgres, the read passes such a struct to inspect/1, which runs the Inspect implementation of the struct module that the attacker selected. A chain of struct modules from ecto and db_connection then calls a function that the cursor names, which permits OS command execution. An %Ash.Query.Function.Fragment{} inside an %Ash.CiString{} value is written into the SQL query as raw text.

This issue affects ash: from 3.31.3 before 3.38.0.

ex_aws_s3 builds x-amz-meta-* request headers by interpolating user-supplied object metadata directly into header names and values without any validation. If the configured HTTP adapter does not neutralize header values before writing them to the socket, the embedded CRLF starts a new header line, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary headers into (or split) the HTTP request the library sends to the S3 endpoint. This is an HTTP header (CRLF) injection leading to HTTP request splitting. The practical impact depends on the HTTP adapter, and no authentication is required beyond the ability to influence object metadata.

This issue affects ex_aws_s3: from 2.0.0 before 2.6.0.

items.summary:
Use of RSA Algorithm without OAEP vulnerability in ex-aws ex_aws_kms (ExAws.KMS module) causes callers who import external key material to wrap their secret KMS key material with the deprecated PKCS#1 v1.5 padding scheme by default.

This vulnerability is associated with program file lib/ex_aws/kms.ex and program routine ExAws.KMS.get_parameters_for_import/3.

ExAws.KMS.get_parameters_for_import/3 defaults its wrapping_algorithm argument to "RSAES_PKCS1_V1_5". AWS KMS returns this value as the WrappingAlgorithm for the import operation, and it dictates the RSA padding scheme the caller uses to wrap (RSA-encrypt) their secret key material before calling ImportKeyMaterial. AWS KMS also supports the stronger RSAES_OAEP_SHA_1 and RSAES_OAEP_SHA_256 schemes. By defaulting to RSAES_PKCS1_V1_5, the library steers callers who do not explicitly override the argument toward the weakest of the three. PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption padding is susceptible to Bleichenbacher adaptive chosen-ciphertext (padding oracle) attacks, which can recover the wrapped plaintext without the private key given an oracle that reveals whether a decrypted value was validly padded. Because the unwrap happens inside AWS KMS, which does not expose a padding oracle, the practical exploitability is low and this is a defense-in-depth weakness. Callers can avoid the weak default by explicitly passing "RSAES_OAEP_SHA_256" (or "RSAES_OAEP_SHA_1") as the wrapping algorithm.

This issue affects ex_aws_kms: from 2.1.0 before 2.7.0.

This issue affects ex_aws_dynamo: from 2.0.0 before 4.3.0.

This vulnerability is associated with program files lib/ex_aws/request/url.ex and program routines ExAws.Request.Url.build/2, ExAws.Request.Url.sanitize/2 and ExAws.Request.Url.get_path/2.

ex_aws does not percent-encode reserved characters in S3 object keys when it assembles the request URL. A literal ? in an object key survives unencoded: build/2 inserts the operation path verbatim and URI.to_string/1 emits it without encoding, and sanitize/2 then splits the flattened URL on the first ?, treating everything after it as the query string. Because the split runs before uri_encode is applied to the path, the ? is never neutralized, and the recovered query is re-inserted without any encoding.

An attacker who controls part of an object key (for example a download or upload keyed by a user-supplied filename) can therefore truncate the key past application-appended suffixes, causing the request to address a different object than the application intended, and can inject live S3 sub-resource operations (such as ?acl, ?tagging or ?versions) into the request. The manipulated URL is signed and transmitted normally, so the tampering is authorized like any legitimate request.

This issue affects ex_aws: from 2.1.2 before 2.8.0.

items.summary:
Relative path traversal in ex_aws allows an attacker who controls an S3 object key to escape the intended bucket or key prefix.

When ex_aws builds a path-style S3 request, ExAws.Operation.S3.add_bucket_to_path/2 in lib/ex_aws/operation/s3.ex joins the bucket name and the object key into a single path string and then normalizes it, collapsing . and .. segments the way a filesystem path would. Because the bucket is the first segment of the combined string, a leading ../ in the object key pops the bucket off the path. With bucket mybucket and a key of ../victim/secret.txt, the combined /mybucket/../victim/secret.txt normalizes to /victim/secret.txt, so the request (signed with the application's own credentials) is sent to bucket victim. The same mechanism collapses ../ within a key, defeating any isolation an application enforces by prepending a trusted prefix.

Only the default path-style configuration is affected; requests built with virtual_host: true do not run this normalization. Because S3 treats object keys as opaque and does not resolve .. itself, the client-side normalization introduces a traversal that would not otherwise exist. Any application that derives an S3 object key from untrusted input and relies on the bucket, or a key prefix, as a tenant or trust boundary is exposed to cross-bucket or cross-prefix read and write, depending on the operation and the credentials' permissions.

This issue affects ex_aws: from 2.1.7 before 2.8.0.

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in ex_aws (instance metadata token provider).

This vulnerability is associated with program files lib/ex_aws/instance_meta_token_provider.ex and program routines ExAws.InstanceMetaTokenProvider.request_token/1 and ExAws.InstanceMetaTokenProvider.get/1.

ex_aws requests its IMDSv2 session token from the link-local metadata endpoint (http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token) with HTTP redirect following enabled. Because the token request follows 3xx redirects and does not restrict the redirect target to the link-local range, an attacker who can influence the response to the metadata request (for example an on-segment neighbor spoofing the link-local address) can answer with a redirect to an arbitrary host. The library follows the redirect and accepts the arbitrary host's response body as the IMDSv2 session token, caching it and sending it as the x-aws-ec2-metadata-token header on every subsequent metadata and credential request.

This issue affects ex_aws: from 2.3.0 before 2.8.0.

items.summary:
Use of Externally-Controlled Input to Select Classes or Code ('Unsafe Reflection') vulnerability in elixir-ecto db_connection allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code via a forged DBConnection.Stream or DBConnection.PrepareStream struct. The Enumerable implementations of both structs in lib/db_connection.ex run with the options stored in the struct. The :log option accepts a {module, function, arguments} tuple, which DBConnection applies. When code enumerates a forged struct, DBConnection calls the chosen function.

This issue is not exploitable in db_connection alone. It is, in theory, a vulnerability of the downstream component. The root cause is a component that decodes untrusted input with :erlang.binary_to_term/2 and does not restrict which terms the result contains. The :safe option does not reject structs, and these structs contain only plain terms. Structs of other libraries can possibly lead to the same result, so a component that decodes untrusted terms stays at risk independently of db_connection. This record exists because the struct was used in attacks on such components.

This issue affects db_connection: from 1.1.0 before 2.10.3.

items.summary:
Out-of-bounds Read vulnerability in the external term format decoder in Erlang OTP erts allows an attacker who controls the input to binary_to_term/1,2 to read memory after the input, and to change one byte there, via a FLOAT_EXT term without a terminating zero byte. decoded_size in erts/emulator/beam/external.c checks only that the 31 bytes of the FLOAT_EXT field are present. dec_term then passes the field to sys_chars_to_double, which scans to a NUL byte without a length limit. When the field has no NUL, the scan continues into the bytes after the field, and those bytes change the decoded float. When the radix character is found after the field and strtod does not accept it, sys_chars_to_double overwrites that byte (a , becomes a .). The VM can fault if the scan reaches an unmapped page.

The safe option does not prevent this. enif_binary_to_term() and the distribution protocol reach the same decoder, and distribution is assumed to run on trusted networks only. The write is limited to the one radix byte. No arbitrary write or code execution was shown.

This issue affects OTP from OTP 17.0 before OTP 27.3.4.20, OTP 28.5.0.9, and OTP 29.1.3, corresponding to erts from 6.0 before 15.2.7.15, 16.4.0.8, and 17.1.2. Whether OTP before OTP 17.0, corresponding to erts before 6.0, is affected is unknown.

items.summary:
Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in Erlang OTP inets (httpd_script_env module) allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust the atom table of an httpd server that serves ESI scripts.

When mod_esi builds the environment for an ESI callback, httpd_script_env:http_env_element/3 checks that a request header name already exists as an atom, then creates the atom http_<header-name> with list_to_atom/1. Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via unchecked exponent length in binary REAL decoding.

Binary REAL decoding never bounds-checks the exponent length against the available content. items.summary:
Convert::ASN1 versions before 0.37 for Perl allow memory exhaustion via unbounded MSG_PEEK buffer doubling in asn_recv.

asn_recv peeks the socket in a loop, doubling the buffer size on each pass until a tag and length can be decoded. An inverted boolean guard ($tb || rather than $tb &&) prevents the need-more-data exit from firing once a tag byte has been decoded. When asn_decode_length returns no value because the length is absent or incomplete, no exit fires for that case either. MSG_PEEK leaves socket data unconsumed, so each re-peek returns at once while the buffer size doubles.

A single truncated BER header sent to a process calling asn_recv doubles the peek buffer until memory is exhausted. Perl's realloc failure is fatal and not catchable with eval.
